name: factory
intent: Give aggregate creation a single named owner: a factory operation that takes everything needed, validates preconditions (including rules that consult other aggregates or services), and returns a fully valid aggregate — or a typed failure — so no client can assemble an inconsistent object.
problem: Consistent aggregate creation is complex enough to deserve one owner: it often computes several fields from the input, checks invariants that span fields or collaborators (uniqueness, an active plan, a pricing policy) before the object exists, and mints identity. Left to public constructors and scattered callers, each caller assembles a slightly different — and occasionally invalid — object; the same creation rules get duplicated across application services, importers and tests, and can silently drift apart.
context: Tactical domain modelling: entities and aggregates whose invariants span fields or collaborators, creation paths that carry domain meaning (register, open, renew, rehydrate), and rehydration from external or legacy data. Applies to rich object models and to functional cores alike; the strongest case is when construction must consult repositories or domain services that the aggregate itself must not know about.
benefits: Invariant safety at birth: an aggregate exists only in a valid state, and clients cannot forget a rule because they cannot reach the constructor.
Named creation paths in the ubiquitous language (Order.open, Subscription.renew, Agreement.rehydrate) make the intent of every creation visible at the call site.
Construction knowledge is centralized and independently testable instead of duplicated across application services, controllers, importers and tests.
The aggregate stays dependency-free: only the factory knows repositories, domain services or external schemas, so the entity remains unit-testable and persistence-ignorant.
Rehydration and anti-corruption live in one place; external row/DTO shapes are translated in the factory and never leak into the model.
Identity minting and creation events happen consistently for every creation path instead of ad hoc per caller.
tradeoffs: For an aggregate whose construction is plain field assignment, a factory is ceremony — Evans' 'when a constructor is all you need' case; a validating constructor or a language-native named constructor is simpler.

A factory that consults repositories or domain services drifts toward being an application service: I/O, transaction boundaries and policy leak into the domain layer, and the factory is no longer testable without ports.
Creation rules fragment across several named factories, so the aggregate's invariant set is no longer visible in one place and factory rules can drift from the constructor's own checks.

Enforcement depends on the language: where constructors cannot be made non-public (Python, JavaScript, Ruby allocate/Marshal, serializer and ORM reflection paths), the factory remains a documented convention with a known bypass.
The 'always valid' promise is easy to over-apply: contextual rules (can this order be placed?) get pushed into creation, multiplying types and queries instead of moving to a Specification.

Static factory methods — named constructors on the type itself — cannot be substituted in tests unless the type is injected as an interface, making them closer to the service-locator pattern than to a true factory.

Factories add a runtime dispatch point: DI containers resolve dependencies at startup, while factory calls are evaluated on demand; for inexpensive objects the factory call overhead can dominate the creation cost.

participants.responsibility: Owns creation: validates preconditions, mints or accepts identity, constructs the product through its non-public constructor and may raise a creation event, returning a fully valid instance.
Enforces its invariants on every mutation; its constructor is non-public, so the factory is the only way to bring it into existence.
Application service, another aggregate or an anti-corruption layer that needs an instance; it speaks the factory's domain language and never assembles the product field by field.
Repositories, domain services or policies the factory may consult while creating (uniqueness, an active plan, pricing); they are given to the factory, never to the product.

use_cases: Opening an order from a shopping cart: mint an OrderId, reject an empty cart, price the lines through a policy, raise OrderOpened.
Rehydrating aggregates in a repository or anti-corruption layer: translate a row or JSON payload into a valid aggregate without exposing the external shape to the model.
Registering an agreement or starting a subscription only after checking another aggregate or a domain service (the customer exists, the plan is active).
Producing value objects whose invariants span several fields — a DateRange with start <= end, a Money with currency and rounding — as named constructs such as from_period or of.
Establishing test fixtures: object mothers and builders are factories in test scope and should go through the same validated creation paths as production code.

Django model factories: factory_boy produces Model instances for tests; validates model constraints before the ORM bypasses full_clean() on save, so the factory must simulate what the model's clean methods enforce in non-Django contexts.

SQLAlchemy session factories: sessionmaker() is the framework-level factory idiom for database sessions — callers receive consistent instances tuned to an engine, illustrating how frameworks codify the pattern.

Spring bean factories: FactoryBean<T> lets a bean wrap creation of another object (e.g., a connection pool) behind an IoC-managed interface; contrasts with @Bean static factory methods that belong to a @Configuration class.

Java time API value objects: java.time types (OffsetDateTime.of, ofInstant, Instant.ofEpochSecond) are immutable aggregates created exclusively through named static factory operations that validate ranges and derive fields (offset from zone), so every instance is valid by construction.

Swift Foundation URL: init?(string:) is a failable initializer — the documented creation path returns nil rather than constructing an invalid URL, the language-native form of 'no instance exists unless it passed the check'.

Rust newtypes over external data: std::convert::TryFrom is the idiomatic fallible creation operation (try_from -> Result<Self, Error>) for building a validated newtype or aggregate from an untrusted input type, keeping From reserved for conversions that can never produce an invalid value.
avoid_when: Creation is a single constructor call with all inputs already validated — when a constructor is all you need, do not add a factory.
The object is a plain data carrier or DTO with no invariants beyond its field types; a record, struct or newtype is enough.
The new state is reached from an existing aggregate through a normal method (order.add_line) — that is behaviour, not creation.
The 'invalid' input is actually a legitimate domain state (a draft, an unconfirmed booking); model that state instead of rejecting construction with a factory.
Only a different name or a convenience default is wanted: a language-native named constructor or static factory method already covers it without a separate creation owner.

The object's construction is a framework lifecycle concern already handled by the framework (Django ORM rehydration via save(), SQLAlchemy @reconstructor, JPA entity listeners) — adding a factory layer duplicates what the persistence mapper already does.
You only need to decouple from a concrete class in tests: a test seam (partial application, patching, or DI) is lighter than introducing a factory hierarchy.
anti_patterns: Pass-through factory: a factory method that only forwards its arguments to the constructor, adding a layer without enforcing anything.
Public constructor beside the factory: the documented creation path is optional, so invalid instances still get built.
God factory: one creation object that knows every aggregate in the context, coupling all construction rules together.
Factory that persists: calling save or committing a unit of work inside creation, silently mixing factory and application-service responsibilities.
Duplicated rules: the same invariant enforced in factory and constructor, drifting apart until one of them is wrong.
Failure by nil: returning null/None/undefined instead of a typed failure, pushing invalid-object handling onto every caller.
Switch-driven factory: a factory that selects the product type with a switch or if/elif chain — every new product variant requires editing the factory, violating the open-closed principle.

Static-only factory: a factory exposed only as static methods on a concrete class cannot be mocked in tests, substituted at runtime, or injected as a collaborator; it is a service locator in factory clothing.

Factory-of-factories: a registry factory that returns other factories requires every caller to know which sub-factory to ask for, adding indirection without isolating clients from the creation hierarchy.
Factory used as global choke point: a single shared factory instance accessed from everywhere hides which caller triggers which creation path and makes testing ordering-dependent.
design_principles: Single responsibility: creation knowledge is separated from the aggregate's behaviour and from application orchestration.
Encapsulation and information hiding: constructors are non-public; clients interact only through named creation paths.
Intention-revealing interfaces: creation operations are named after the domain's intent (register, renew, rehydrate), not after implementation (createOrder1).
Dependency inversion: the factory depends on repositories and domain services; the aggregate depends on neither.
Fail fast: invalid input is rejected before an object exists, and failures are typed values or exceptions rather than half-built instances.
best_practices: Close the raw path: once a factory owns creation, make the constructor private/protected/internal (or keep fields unexported) so every instance passes the same checks.
Name each creation path after the domain event or intent it represents, one method per path.
Validate everything before minting identity or allocating, so a failed creation leaves nothing half-built and burns no identity.
Keep the aggregate free of factory dependencies: inject repositories and domain services into a standalone factory rather than passing them into the product.
Return a typed failure (Result, Either, throws, error code) instead of nil or a partially initialized object.
Raise creation events in the aggregate method the factory calls; the factory orchestrates inputs, not state transitions.
Test each named creation path directly, with in-memory ports for the collaborators it consults.
Prefer first-class creator functions over class hierarchies when the set of product types is known and fixed — a dict or registry of callables is lighter than a factory subclass.
Use Pydantic or similar validation libraries as 'parse, don't validate' factories in Python: construct a domain model through a validated schema, returning a typed failure on parse error.
For ORMs that reconstruct instances bypassing __init__, add a @reconstructor hook and document that the factory is not bypassed — the ORM produces a structurally valid but factory-unchecked instance.
sources: Evans, E. (2003). Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. Addison-Wesley - Chapter 6, 'The Life Cycle of a Domain Object' (FACTORIES; 'When a Constructor Is All You Need'). https://fabiofumarola.github.io/nosql/readingMaterial/Evans03.pdf

Gamma, E., Helm, R., Johnson, R., Vlissides, J. (1994). Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software. Addison-Wesley - Factory Method (pp. 107-116) and Abstract Factory (pp. 87-96). https://w3sdesign.com/GoF_Design_Patterns_Reference0100.pdf

Martin Fowler - Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection Pattern: distinguishes factory classes from DI containers; notes 'you can make a factory class, but then that just becomes another service instance'. https://martinfowler.com/articles/injection.html

Martin Fowler - Dependency Composition in TypeScript/Node.js: function-first composition via partial application as an alternative to factory classes, productionFactories test seam. https://martinfowler.com/articles/dependency-composition.html

Martin Fowler - Creation Object: reified creation process as a complement to the factory pattern, separating construction knowledge from validity requirements. https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CreationObject.html

Joshua Bloch - Effective Java, Item 1: Consider static factory methods instead of constructors — naming, instance control, and interface-driven design; contrast with GoF factory method. https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/effective-java/9780134685997/

Refactoring Guru - Factory Method Pattern: strict terminology separation (Factory vs creation method vs static creation method vs Simple Factory vs Factory Method vs Abstract Factory), pros/cons. https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/factory-method

Refactoring Guru - Abstract Factory Pattern: product families, applicability, consequences including 'unnecessary complexity and extra work, more difficult to debug and maintain'. https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/abstract-factory

Refactoring Guru - Factory Pattern Comparison: when to use which variant, relationship to Builder and Prototype, dynamic language perspective. https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns/factory-comparison

Peter Norvig - Design Patterns in Dynamic Languages (OOPSLA 1996): Factory Method and Abstract Factory are 2 of the 16/23 GoF patterns that are 'invisible or simpler' in dynamic languages via first-class functions. https://norvig.com/design-patterns/
Scott Seemann / arDalis - Factory Pattern: static factory vs DI, factory vs builder distinction, OCP violation in switch-factories. https://ardalis.com/factory-patterns/
C2 Wiki - Factory Pattern Considered Harmful: early community consensus on factory overuse, needless indirection, and when constructors suffice. https://wiki.c2.com/?FactoryPatternConsideredHarmful

Harry Percival & Bob Gregory - Architecture Patterns with Python (Cosmic Python): aggregate factory in Python, classmethod creation methods on aggregates, standalone factories for repository access. https://www.cosmicpython.com/

Vaughn Vernon - Implementing Domain-Driven Design (IDDD): Chapter 11 Factories — aggregate factory creation rules, factory method on aggregate root, identity assignment. https://www.goodreads.com/book/show/15756869-implementing-domain-driven-design

ProteanHQ - Domain-Driven Design Factory Methods: practical DDD factory patterns for aggregate creation in Python, standalone vs embedded factory tradeoffs. https://docs.proteanhq.com/patterns/factory-methods-for-aggregate-creation/

Django ORM - Model.objects.create(): factory-like bulk creation that bypasses full_clean(), illustrating why domain-layer factories must not assume ORM paths validate the same invariants. https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/ref/models/instances/

SQLAlchemy - sessionmaker as factory: the documented factory idiom for producing scoped sessions and engines. https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/stable/orm/session.html#sqlalchemy.orm.session.sessionmaker

SQLAlchemy - @reconstructor: ORM lifecycle hook for reconstituting aggregates bypassing __init__, relevant to persistence bypassing the factory. https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/stable/orm/mapping_legacy.html#sqlalchemy.orm.reconstructor
Spring Framework - FactoryBean: factory interface for Spring-managed bean creation with pluggable backend; contrasts with @Bean static factory methods. https://spring.io/spring-framework

Eric Evans - Domain-Driven Design, Pearson official sample chapter (Ch. 6, 'The Life Cycle of a Domain Object'): FACTORIES rules — creation operations must be atomic, pass everything needed in one interaction, hide interior construction; 'When a Constructor Is All You Need'. https://ptgmedia.pearsoncmg.com/images/9780321125217/samplepages/0321125215.pdf

Java SE API - java.time.OffsetDateTime: immutable value aggregates constructed exclusively via named static factory operations (of, ofInstant) that validate fields and derive the offset from the zone. https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/java/time/OffsetDateTime.html

Apple Developer Documentation - Foundation URL.init(string:): failable initializer returning nil for unparseable input — the creation path never yields an invalid URL instance. https://developer.apple.com/documentation/foundation/url/init(string:)

The Swift Programming Language - Initialization: failable initializers (init?) as the language-native fallible factory, failing to nil on invalid parameters or missing resources. https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/initialization/

Rust std::convert - TryFrom: the idiomatic fallible conversion trait (try_from -> Result<Self, Self::Error>) for validated construction from an untrusted input type, with From reserved for infallible conversions. https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/convert/trait.TryFrom.html

Steve Yegge - Execution in the Kingdom of Nouns: criticism of the Java 'factory school' — wrapping every action in factory/proxy classes yields verbose, action-averse indirection where first-class functions would do. https://steve-yegge.blogspot.com/2006/03/execution-in-kingdom-of-nouns.html
